content: In ancient India, builders of grand temples used precise directions based on the sun's path, calling the left side 'Vama' (वाम) and the right side 'Dakshina' (दक्षिण). Have you ever wondered how a pilot finds the right runway today? It all starts with these two ancient concepts: Left and Right!
Imagine you are standing in a dark room and someone tells you to 'go that way'. How would you know which way to go? What would happen if we didn't have words for directions?

content.title: The Left Hand 'L' Trick
content.description: Hold both your hands in front of you with the back of your hands facing you. Extend your thumbs. The hand that makes a perfect 'L' shape is your Left hand!

content: The words Left and Right are called 'Directions'. The English word 'Direction' comes from the Latin 'directio', meaning 'setting straight'. In Sanskrit, it is 'Disha' (दिशा). Directions help us set our path straight compared to our own body.

definition: A word used to tell someone where to go or where something is, like left, right, up, or down.

question: When you hold both hands up, which hand's thumb and index finger make a perfect 'L' shape?

content: Many students get confused when someone is facing them. Remember, if your teacher is facing you, their left side is opposite to your right side! Directions flip when you face each other.
Take a moment to look around your room. Close your eyes and try to remember: What object is exactly to your right? What is to your left? Explain how you know this to your sibling or parent.
Knowing left and right connects to many things! In Science, we learn that our heart is slightly on the left side of our chest. In Geography, knowing left and right is the first step to reading maps!
Tell students to look at their shoes. Often, shoes have a slight curve that points inward. This can also help them identify the left shoe from the right shoe!

Mini Challenge: Play 'Robot Commander'. Ask a friend to be the robot. Give them commands using only 'Turn Left', 'Turn Right', and 'Step Forward' to navigate them around a chair. Now you are thinking like a real programmer!
